subject: surgery
title: Infected Pancreatic Necrosis and Step-Up Approach

steps.tx: A severe local complication developing in approximately twenty percent of patients suffering from acute pancreatitis is **infected pancreatic necrosis**. Non-viable, devitalized pancreatic parenchyma or peripancreatic retroperitoneal fat becomes colonized by translocating enteric Gram-negative bacilli such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella. Infection typically supervenes two to four weeks following the onset of pancreatitis, triggering late-onset sepsis and multi-organ failure.
steps.say: Infected pancreatic necrosis develops two to four weeks into acute pancreatitis from bacterial translocation, driving severe late sepsis.

vis.alt: Computed tomography diagram showing walled-off pancreatic necrosis and minimally invasive transgastric drainage catheters.
vis.caption: Walled-off pancreatic necrosis: encapsulated retroperitoneal necrotic collection managed by drainage. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography is the gold standard imaging modality for demonstrating pancreatic parenchymal non-enhancement representing necrotizing pancreatitis. While sterile necrosis can be managed conservatively with supportive intensive care, the presence of gas bubbles within the retroperitoneal necrotic collection confirms the definitive diagnosis of **pancreatic infection**. In questionable cases, fine-needle aspiration for Gram stain and culture can be selectively utilized.
steps.say: Extraluminal retroperitoneal gas within non-enhancing pancreatic parenchyma on contrast CT confirms infected necrosis.

steps.tx: Historically, infected necrosis mandated emergency open surgical debridement, but early open necrosectomy carried disastrous operative mortality rates approaching forty percent. Contemporary surgical practice delays intervention until the necrotic debris encapsulates into walled-off necrosis, which requires at least four weeks. This delayed strategy minimizes intraoperative haemorrhage and dramatically improves outcomes within the framework of the **step-up approach**.
steps.say: Delaying intervention until necrotic tissue encapsulates into walled-off necrosis at four weeks significantly reduces operative morbidity and mortality.

vis.alt: Pathological diagram illustrating transition from acute peripancreatic fluid collections to encapsulated walled-off necrosis.
vis.caption: Evolution of acute necrotic collections: progressive encapsulation over four weeks into walled-off pancreatic necrosis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The randomized Dutch PANTER trial revolutionized the management paradigm of infected necrosis by validating the minimally invasive **PANTER trial protocol**. The first step entails percutaneous radiologically guided catheter drainage or endoscopic transluminal transmural drainage of infected collections. Remarkably, primary catheter drainage alone successfully resolves sepsis and obviates the need for any subsequent surgical necrosectomy in up to thirty-five percent of patients.
steps.say: The PANTER trial demonstrated that primary catheter drainage resolves infected necrosis in over one-third of patients without requiring surgical debridement.

steps.tx: If the patient fails to show clinical and biochemical improvement within seventy-two hours following initial catheter drainage, the protocol escalates to minimally invasive surgical **necrosectomy**. Rather than performing open laparotomy, surgical access is obtained by dilating the established percutaneous drain tract under fluoroscopic guidance to introduce an operative nephroscope, a procedure termed video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement.
steps.say: Patients failing to improve following initial drainage undergo minimally invasive necrosectomy via video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement.

steps.tx: During video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement, gentle suction and grasping forceps are utilized to tease away loose, non-viable black necrotic tissue while strictly avoiding forceful avulsion of adherent parenchyma. Vigorous traction risks catastrophic avulsion of major retroperitoneal vessels, particularly the splenic vein and **gastroduodenal artery**. Following debridement, large wide-bore irrigation drains are placed to maintain continuous postoperative closed-circuit lavage.
steps.say: Necrosectomy requires gentle removal of loose necrotic tissue while avoiding aggressive traction that could lacerate major retroperitoneal blood vessels.

steps.tx: Alternatively, when walled-off necrosis directly abuts the posterior gastric wall, endoscopic ultrasound-guided transmural drainage using lumen-apposing metal stents followed by direct endoscopic **necrosectomy** has emerged as a frontline option. Under carbon dioxide insufflation, an endoscope is advanced directly through the stent into the necrotic cavity. Dead tissue is extracted systematically using snares and baskets under continuous endoscopic vision.
steps.say: Endoscopic necrosectomy utilizes lumen-apposing metal stents to debride retroperitoneal necrosis through the stomach wall without skin incisions.

steps.tx: A vital delayed complication of necrotizing pancreatitis following successful drainage is the disconnected pancreatic duct syndrome. When central parenchymal necrosis destroys a segment of the neck or body of the pancreas, the viable upstream pancreatic tail is functionally disconnected from the duodenum. This isolated viable segment continues secreting enzymes, causing chronic recurrent fluid collections or a persistent external **pancreatic fistula** requiring definitive distal pancreatectomy or internal Roux-en-Y drainage.
steps.say: Disconnected pancreatic duct syndrome occurs when central necrosis isolates a viable secreting tail, producing persistent fluid collections or external fistulas.
